questions.question: Which statement best describes heart failure?
choices: It is defined only by a low ejection fraction
It is a clinical syndrome involving structural/functional cardiac abnormality and symptoms/signs
It is the same as isolated leg edema
It can be diagnosed from one medication list
questions.explanation: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome; ejection fraction helps classify phenotype but does not alone establish or exclude the diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate first step when a patient with known heart failure reports new dyspnea and edema?
choices: Assume heart failure is the only cause
Compare with baseline and assess congestion, perfusion, triggers, and alternative diagnoses
Refill all medications without assessment
Ignore symptoms if ejection fraction was previously preserved
questions.explanation: New symptoms require trajectory assessment and a differential, because pulmonary, renal, infectious, ischemic, and rhythm problems may mimic or precipitate decompensation.

questions.question: Which finding is most concerning for hypoperfusion in heart failure?
choices: Cool extremities with hypotension and altered mentation
Stable daily weight
A routine vaccination question
Mild chronic ankle swelling without change
questions.explanation: Hypotension, cool extremities, and altered mentation can indicate poor systemic perfusion and require urgent assessment.

questions.question: What is the primary role of a diuretic in congested heart failure?
choices: Relieve sodium/water congestion and symptoms
Replace all disease-modifying therapy
Treat every cause of dyspnea
Eliminate the need for follow-up
questions.explanation: Diuretics are used primarily for symptom relief from congestion; they do not substitute for individualized disease-modifying care when indicated.

questions.question: Which issue should be reviewed before changing chronic heart-failure therapy?
choices: Only the diagnosis date
Blood pressure, volume status, renal function/electrolytes when appropriate, adherence, access, and adverse effects
Only the patient’s age
Only a previous echocardiogram
questions.explanation: Safe therapy adjustment requires current clinical context, monitoring, and attention to adherence and access barriers.

questions.question: Which is a common trigger for heart-failure decompensation?
choices: Missed medications, NSAID exposure, infection, arrhythmia, or ischemia
A normal follow-up visit
Correct inhaler technique
Stable access to medication
questions.explanation: Decompensation commonly has a precipitant; medication issues, infection, arrhythmia, ischemia, renal dysfunction, and other factors should be sought.

questions.question: Why does preserved ejection fraction not rule out heart failure?
choices: HFpEF can involve impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures despite preserved EF
Ejection fraction never has clinical value
Only HFrEF causes symptoms
HFpEF always has low EF
questions.explanation: HFpEF can cause significant dyspnea and congestion through impaired filling and elevated filling pressures despite a preserved EF.

questions.question: Which presentation requires emergency evaluation rather than routine outpatient follow-up?
choices: Severe respiratory distress with hypoxemia and hypotension
A stable patient asking about a scale
A planned cardiology appointment
No change from baseline
questions.explanation: Severe distress, hypoxemia, hypotension, shock, acute pulmonary edema, or instability require emergency-level evaluation.

questions.question: When is expedited cardiology or heart-failure-team involvement appropriate?
choices: Recurrent hospitalization, uncertain etiology, escalating diuretic needs, or complex disease
A single uncomplicated refill request
A stable baseline visit only
No symptoms and no clinical questions
questions.explanation: Complex, recurrent, advanced, or uncertain heart failure benefits from timely specialty collaboration.

questions.question: What is the FNP-level heart-failure management principle?
choices: Treat the medication list rather than the patient
Integrate phenotype, baseline, trajectory, congestion, perfusion, triggers, access, and safety
Use the same plan for every patient
Rely only on ejection fraction
questions.explanation: High-quality longitudinal care integrates physiology, function, objective data, context, and safe disposition.
